description:
We are VILNIUS TECH AI undergraduates and hackathon finalists (Hack4Vilnius) bringing strong technical execution in Python, C++, and MATLAB. We combine rapid prototyping with clean system design to build impactful solutions.

We are looking for driven teammates passionate about space tech, data, or design to join us in building a winning project for the NASA Space Apps Hackathon. Let’s build something out of this world!
summary:
BioMatrix is a web app that lets astronauts check their own health and act on it, even when Earth is too far away to help in real time. On a Mars mission, a message to Earth and back can take 40 minutes, so the crew needs onboard support, not just charts for doctors on the ground.

The astronaut enters daily health values by hand or from standard Bluetooth devices. A see-through body map then shows each organ zone in green, amber or red, with NASA-sourced guidance on why space causes the problem and what to do. A 4-level triage decides when to use self-care, ask the crew medical officer or contact flight surgeons, and adapts to the mission (ISS, Moon, Mars, rover).

Our Autonomy Copilot goes further. It links body, cabin-air and space-weather signals into one likely cause, learns each astronaut's personal normal to warn before limits are crossed, gives a GO/NO-GO for spacewalks, and guides the crew one step at a time. A live heart monitor catches sudden changes within seconds. Every action goes into a flight surgeon report, so Earth stays informed even when it cannot intervene.
details:
What it does
BioMatrix is a web app that helps astronauts check their own health and act on the result when Earth is too far away to help in real time. On a Mars mission, a message to Earth and back can take 40 minutes or more, so the crew needs help deciding what to do on board. Charts for doctors on the ground can’t do that. BioMatrix covers the full loop the challenge asks for: gather indicators, evaluate them, act on them, and know when to escalate.

How it works

  1. Gather: the astronaut does a daily check-in of 15 indicators (blood pressure, heart rate, SpO2, breathing rate, cabin CO2, glucose, hydration, temperature, sleep, mood, reaction time, vision, exercise, radiation dose, solar particle events) plus symptoms. Each value has step-by-step help on how to measure it. Values can be typed in or filled in automatically from standard Bluetooth health devices (heart-rate straps, blood-pressure cuffs, thermometers, pulse oximeters). A 15-second reaction test helps spot fatigue.
  2. Evaluate: a see-through body map shows five zones (neuro-ocular, cardiopulmonary, metabolic, musculoskeletal, immune and radiation) in green, amber or red. Clicking a zone zooms in and shows the live values, the linked NASA hazards, why space causes the problem, and what to do about it.
  3. Act and escalate: a 4-level triage (Nominal, Self-Care, Crew Medical Officer, Transmit to Flight Surgeons) changes with the mission environment (ISS, Lunar Base, Mars Transit, Pressurized Rover). On Mars, self-care steps come first because Earth can’t answer quickly.
  4. Autonomy Copilot: for common combinations, it links body, cabin-air and space-weather signals to one likely cause. For example, high CO2 with a headache and slow reactions means “fix the air and warn the whole crew”. It shows what it ruled out, and it settles conflicting steps (a solar-storm shelter comes before moving to cleaner air). From the astronaut’s own check-ins, it learns their usual values and flags unusual changes before a limit is crossed. It also estimates trends, gives a GO / CAUTION / NO-GO for spacewalks and safety-critical work, and guides the crew one step at a time with timers.
  5. Live heart monitor: reads a Bluetooth heart-rate strap about every second and catches sudden jumps or drops. A change is confirmed over several readings, so a loose strap doesn’t raise a false alarm. It switches between nominal cruise, drift watch and burst capture modes, which shows how much data it would send to Earth in each case. A clearly labelled training drill lets the crew practise emergencies without touching real data.
  6. Report and explain: one click creates a flight surgeon report with readings, triage, the onboard analysis, every action taken and the last 7 check-ins. It can be printed, saved as a PDF, downloaded as text or copied. An AI assistant (Google Gemini) explains the results in plain words, using only the facts in the app. With no internet, the app writes its own short summary instead and marks it as not AI-generated.

Benefits

  • Astronauts understand their health at a glance instead of reading raw numbers.
  • Clear guidance on what to do now and when to call the crew medical officer or Earth.
  • Less to think about under stress: one likely cause, one decision, one step at a time.
  • Flight surgeons get a complete, structured report, even with a long communication delay.
  • Daily routine support: history charts, reminders to measure again and a check-in streak.
  • Private by design: data stays in the browser, and after the first visit the app works fully offline.

Intended impact
BioMatrix is built for future Moon and Mars missions, where crews will have to handle medical problems with little help from Earth. The same approach can help people in other isolated places where a doctor is far away: polar research stations, ships, submarines, offshore platforms and remote communities.

Tools and technologies

  • React 18, TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind CSS (web app)
  • Recharts (charts) and Lucide (icons)
  • Web Bluetooth API with the official Bluetooth SIG health services (Heart Rate, Blood Pressure, Health Thermometer, Pulse Oximeter)
  • Service Worker and Web App Manifest (offline use and install to home screen)
  • Vercel (hosting and a serverless function) and the Google Gemini API (AI explanation)
  • Hardware: any standard Bluetooth health device; manual entry works without any device
  • Playwright for automated testing of the interface

How it is creative
Most health dashboards show live charts to doctors on Earth. BioMatrix is built for the opposite case, where the crew is on its own. It connects body and habitat signals to find a shared cause and compares each astronaut with their own usual values as well as fixed limits. It turns the result into a GO / NO-GO decision and a step-by-step plan, and it adjusts its rules to the mission and its communication delay. It also shows how much data it would send to Earth: one summary a minute when things are stable, every reading during an emergency.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific accuracy: the main limits are checked against NASA, CSA and medical sources (Mayo Clinic, CDC, American Heart Association, American Lung Association and others), and the app links to them. The amber “caution” ranges and the Copilot and alarm rules are our own design, built on those limits.
  • Safety: the app gives guidance, not a diagnosis. The flight surgeon makes medical decisions. Training-drill data is kept separate from real data.
  • Communication delay and crew autonomy on Moon and Mars missions.
  • Mental load: colour coding, plain language and one step at a time.
  • Privacy: no accounts, data stored only in the browser, and only today’s values (no name) are sent when the AI button is pressed.
  • Devices: works on computers and phones, with or without sensors.
